attempts.raw_response: They moved into the property with their young daughter, and a son was born in 1954. By 1955, the marriage had deteriorated, and Mr Gissing left the family home. He subsequently sought to recover possession of the property, claiming it was solely his under the conveyance. Mrs Gissing disputed this, arguing that her financial contribution of £220 entitled her to a share in the beneficial ownership. The case came before the courts, which had to determine whether a resulting trust had been created in her favour despite the property being registered in her husband's name alone. The judge examined the circumstances of the purchase and the parties' intentions at the time of acquisition, considering the significant personal contribution made by Mrs Gissing toward establishing their family home.

pair.human_continuation:
Mr Gissing always paid the mortgage instalments, but left to live with another woman in 1961. She claimed he told her then the house was hers. She succeeded in 1966 in getting a divorce on grounds of his adultery, with a maintenance order but later reduced to 1s a year, and she brought an action that she would be entitled to an equitable interest in the home.

Judgment

Court of Appeal
The majority of the Court of Appeal held that Mrs Gissing was entitled to an equitable interest in the home. Lord Denning MR held that Mrs Gissing was entitled to a half equitable interest in the property, because the home was acquired as a joint venture, even though she contributed no money directly to buying the property.

Mrs Gissing spent £220 of her own money on buying furniture and the laying of the lawn.
